items.prompt: Which receptor class primarily responds to tissue-damaging or potentially damaging stimuli?
items.rationale: Nociceptors respond to potentially damaging mechanical, thermal, or chemical conditions and contribute to pain signalling.

targetedFeedback.c: Chemoreceptors respond to chemical conditions such as dissolved molecules or gas concentrations.
targetedFeedback.d: Mechanoreceptors respond to deformation such as pressure, stretch, vibration, or sound-related movement.

items.prompt: A learner compares two-point discrimination on a fingertip and forearm. Which variable should be kept consistent?

choices.b: The separation distances and application procedure

items.rationale: Using the same distances, pressure, timing, and response procedure makes body region the meaningful comparison.

targetedFeedback.a: Body region is the independent variable being compared.
targetedFeedback.c: The measured discrimination response is the dependent variable, not a condition to hold fixed.
targetedFeedback.d: A prediction is recorded before the test but is not an experimental condition.

items.prompt: A participant reports two points at 8 mm on the fingertip but only one point at 8 mm on the forearm. Which explanation is most defensible?

choices.a: The fingertip likely has denser receptive fields or finer neural representation for this task.
choices.b: The forearm has no sensory receptors.
choices.c: The result proves every person has the same threshold.
choices.d: The fingertip response was endocrine rather than neural.

items.rationale: Finer spatial discrimination is consistent with smaller or denser receptive fields and greater neural representation, while one trial does not establish a universal threshold.

targetedFeedback.b: The forearm has sensory receptors; its spatial resolution is simply lower in this observation.
targetedFeedback.c: Individual variation and procedure limit generalization from one participant.
targetedFeedback.d: Tactile transduction and rapid reporting are neural sensory processes.

items.prompt: Which sequence correctly traces light before neural signals leave the eye?

choices.a: Cornea → pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve

items.rationale: Light is refracted by the cornea, passes through the pupil and lens, and reaches the retina, where transduction begins before signals leave through the optic nerve.

targetedFeedback.b: The optic nerve carries neural output after retinal processing, not incoming light.
targetedFeedback.c: Light reaches the retina after passing the cornea, pupil, and lens.
targetedFeedback.d: The optic nerve is not a transparent optical structure in the incoming light path.

items.prompt: A person can see dim objects off to the side but has difficulty distinguishing their colour. Which retinal pattern best explains this?

choices.a: Peripheral rods are sensitive in dim light but do not support colour vision.
choices.b: Cones in the optic nerve detect sound.
choices.d: The blind spot has the highest cone density.

items.rationale: Rods are numerous in peripheral retina and are highly light-sensitive, whereas cone pathways support colour and detailed vision, especially near the fovea.

targetedFeedback.b: Cones are retinal photoreceptors; the optic nerve carries output and does not detect sound.
targetedFeedback.c: The lens focuses light but does not contain photoreceptors.
targetedFeedback.d: The blind spot lacks photoreceptors because the optic nerve exits there.

items.prompt: A corrective lens improves distance focus but not retinal-cell damage. Which claim best evaluates the technology?

choices.a: It can alter refraction, but it cannot replace photoreceptor transduction.
choices.b: It cures every cause of vision loss.
choices.c: It sends action potentials directly into the lens.
choices.d: It works because the blind spot becomes a fovea.

items.rationale: A corrective lens changes the path of light to improve focus; functioning retinal cells and neural pathways are still required for transduction and perception.

targetedFeedback.b: Vision problems have different mechanisms, and refraction correction does not repair retinal damage.
targetedFeedback.c: The lens is optical tissue; action potentials occur in neural cells.
targetedFeedback.d: The optic-disc blind spot does not transform into the cone-rich fovea.

items.prompt: Which structure converts vibration in cochlear fluid into receptor signals?

choices.a: Hair cells in the organ of Corti

items.rationale: Movement of the basilar membrane bends hair-cell stereocilia in the organ of Corti, producing receptor changes that influence auditory nerve activity.

targetedFeedback.b: The ossicles transmit and amplify mechanical vibration but do not perform the cochlear receptor transduction.
targetedFeedback.c: Semicircular canals detect rotational acceleration for equilibrium.
targetedFeedback.d: The Eustachian tube helps equalize middle-ear pressure.

items.prompt: A synthetic audiogram shows higher thresholds at high frequencies than at low frequencies. What does the graph support?

choices.a: More sound level was required to detect the high-frequency tones in this dataset.
choices.b: The person definitely has one named disorder.
choices.c: High frequencies were heard better than low frequencies.
choices.d: The semicircular canals caused the threshold pattern.

items.rationale: A higher hearing threshold means a greater sound level was required for detection; an audiogram pattern alone does not establish one cause.

targetedFeedback.b: A threshold pattern needs clinical context and other evidence before a cause can be identified.
targetedFeedback.c: Higher thresholds indicate poorer sensitivity, not better hearing.
targetedFeedback.d: Semicircular canals support equilibrium; cochlear and auditory pathways determine tone thresholds.

items.prompt: Why is playing increasing browser tones until a learner reports hearing them unsuitable as a required course test?

choices.a: Device output is uncalibrated and increasing sound can create risk, so supplied clinical-style data are safer and more valid.
choices.b: Sound cannot be represented as data.
choices.d: Only hormones can affect sensory responses.

items.rationale: Uncalibrated speakers and listening environments cannot produce valid thresholds, and escalating volume creates avoidable safety risk; supplied data meet the reasoning goal.

targetedFeedback.b: Audiograms and other measurements represent sound-response evidence quantitatively.
targetedFeedback.c: Hearing sensitivity commonly differs across frequencies.
targetedFeedback.d: Hearing begins with mechanical and neural sensory processes, though health factors can influence them.

items.prompt: Photoperiod is best defined as which environmental information?

choices.a: The duration of light and darkness in a daily cycle
choices.c: The concentration of glucose in urine
choices.d: The speed of one action potential

items.rationale: Photoperiod is the relative duration of light and darkness and can provide seasonal timing information to biological systems.

targetedFeedback.b: Sound loudness is an auditory stimulus, not photoperiod.
targetedFeedback.d: Action-potential speed does not define the light-dark cycle.

items.prompt: A dataset shows activity begins earlier as sunset occurs earlier, but temperature also falls. What is the main limitation?

choices.a: Photoperiod and temperature changed together, so their effects are confounded.
choices.c: The pattern proves temperature has no effect.
choices.d: A correlation always establishes one mechanism.

items.rationale: When two plausible explanatory variables change together, the dataset cannot isolate which one produced the activity shift.

targetedFeedback.b: Time and activity can be measured; the problem is interpretation of co-varying factors.
targetedFeedback.c: The dataset cannot rule temperature out because temperature also changed.
targetedFeedback.d: Correlation can guide hypotheses but does not by itself identify a causal mechanism.

items.prompt: Which evidence brief most responsibly evaluates a sensory-assistive technology?

choices.a: It names the mechanism, measured benefit, limitations, risks, access issues, and evidence source.
choices.b: It calls the device revolutionary and lists no comparison group.
choices.c: It assumes every user values the same outcome.
choices.d: It treats one testimonial as proof of universal effectiveness.

items.rationale: A responsible STS evaluation connects mechanism to measured outcomes and considers uncertainty, safety, access, and affected users.

targetedFeedback.b: Promotional language without comparative evidence does not establish effectiveness.
targetedFeedback.c: Users can value outcomes differently, so perspectives and context matter.
targetedFeedback.d: A testimonial is useful experience evidence but cannot establish universal effect on its own.
